# Abstract

This study reconstructs the demographic trajectory, macro-spatial distribution and settlement systems of mediaeval Turan and Transoxiana (*Mawarannahr*) from the fragmentation of Late Antiquity in 500AD to the eve of the Mongol conquest in 1219AD. Across nine provinces encompassing 3.890.946 km² (65.332 five-arcminute raster cells), aggregate population expanded from 3,55M (3.550.000) in 500AD to 4,1M (4.100.000) in 650AD, climbing to 4,45M (4.450.000) by 800AD following the Arab-Muslim conquest. During the Samanid Golden Age, the integration of Transoxiana into the wider Islamic mercantile ecumene, coupled with Watson's mediaeval Islamic green revolution and intensive irrigation engineering along the Zarafshan, Kashkadarya, Amu Darya and Syr Darya, lifted population to 5,55M (5.550.000) by 950AD [@MirMakhamad2023Testing; @MirMakhamad2024Agricultur; @kyzy2025Religious]. Subsequent nomadic sedentarisation and pastoralist state formation under the Karakhanid Khaganate in Semirechye and Ferghana, paired with the imperial expansion of the Great Seljuk Empire in Khurasan and the Khwarazmshah Empire in Gurganj, propelled regional headcount to 6,35M in 1100AD, 6,85M in 1200AD and a pre-Mongol zenith of 6,95M (6.950.000) in 1219AD [@Knar2024Turkic; @Roberts2024Using; @Sharipbayeva2026Geopolitic]. Headcounts are calibrated against 1.029 catalogued mediaeval settlements led by Merv (150.000), Samarkand (120.000), Bukhara (100.000), Kunya-Urgench (95.000), Old Termez (50.000), Tashkent (48.000), Otrar (40.000), Khujand (38.000), Taraz (32.000) and Balasagun (32.000), integrated with Paciorek-Schervish non-stationary Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$, $\tau_1 = 1{,}50$) kriging across 442 domestic catchments.

# Background

## Environmental Ecology, Fluvial Corridors and Irrigation Oases

The human geography of mediaeval Turan and Transoxiana was dictated by stark biophysical contrasts between expansive arid depressions and hyper-productive riverine oases fed by glacial meltwater from the Pamir, Tian Shan and Hindu Kush massifs [@Franklin2023Archaeolog; @Roberts2024Using]. Covering 3.890.946 km², the domain is bounded by the Caspian Sea on the west, the southern margins of the Kopet Dag and northern Afghanistan on the south, the high alpine ranges of the Pamir and Tian Shan on the east, and the semi-arid Kazakh steppe on the north. Precipitation across the internal plains rarely exceeds 100 to 200 millimetres annually, rendering rainfed cereal agriculture impossible outside narrow piedmont strips in Ferghana, Chach and Semirechye [@MirMakhamad2023Testing; @Elemanova2025Channels].

Consequently, sedentary civilisation was concentrated along endorheic fluvial corridors. The Amu Darya (classical Oxus, Arabic *Jayhun*) and Syr Darya (Jaxartes, *Sayhun*) carried vast volumes of water across the Kyzylkum and Karakum deserts toward the Aral Sea delta [@Ilniyazovich2023Karakalpak]. More critical still for urban agglomeration were smaller rivers that terminated in extensive alluvial fans: the Zarafshan River, which sustained the dense agricultural oases of Samarkand and Bukhara; the Kashkadarya, watering Kesh (Shahrisabz) and Nasaf (Qarshi); the Murghab, supporting the vast delta of Merv; the Hari Rud, draining toward Sarakhs and Tejen; and the Chu and Talas rivers, nurturing the agricultural towns of Semirechye [@Franklin2023Archaeolog; @Roberts2024Using; @Elemanova2025Channels].

The seasonal hydrology of these river systems was synchronised with summer agricultural requirements [@MirMakhamad2023Testing; @Elemanova2025Channels]. High-altitude snow and glacial melt generated peak river discharges between May and July, precisely when high summer temperatures demanded intensive irrigation for cereal and fruit cultivation. The heavy silt load carried by glacial streams, dominated by nutrient-rich loess particles, replenished topsoils continuously across irrigated fields, counteracting salinisation when drainage gradients were properly maintained [@MirMakhamad2023Testing; @MirMakhamad2024Agricultur]. Water allocation was governed by communal institutions headed by water-masters (*mirab*), who enforced strict volumetric rotational schedules through sluice gates (*bends*) and distribution basins [@Elemanova2025Channels; @Pardaev2019Design].

The hydraulic administration of the Murghab delta at Merv represented the pinnacle of mediaeval water engineering in the Iranian-Central Asian borderland [@Roberts2024Using; @Pardaev2019Design]. Upstream of the city, the monumental masonry diversion weir known as the Sultan Band regulated the torrential spring floods of the Murghab, diverting discharge into four primary trunk canals (Hurmuzfarra, Asad, Majan and Raziq) that radiated across the desert fan. According to Al-Istakhri and Al-Muqaddasi, the maintenance of this weir required a permanent municipal workforce of over 10.000 divers and hydraulic labourers (*hashar*), who worked continuously during spring floods to reinforce timber embankments and dredge settling basins [@Roberts2024Using; @Franklin2023Archaeolog].

In the Zarafshan valley, the Dargom canal diverted water from the main river above Samarkand, conveying gravity flow along a high southern terrace to irrigate hundreds of suburban villages before returning drainage to the river downstream [@MirMakhamad2024Agricultur]. Along the lower course approaching Bukhara, the river branched into dozens of distributaries collectively known as the Twelve Canals of Bukhara (including the Nahr al-Qassarin and Vabkent Darya). Extensive mud silt accumulation along canal banks generated linear elevated ridges (*tepe-aryk*) rising three to five metres above adjacent fields, serving as raised pathways and protecting cultivated plots from sudden inundations [@MirMakhamad2023Testing; @Elemanova2025Channels].

In Semirechye, the Chu and Talas rivers supported distinct regional irrigation complexes (*at-aryk*) developed jointly by Sogdian agricultural colonists and sedentarising Karluk Turkic pastoralists [@Elemanova2025Channels; @Anon2024Buran]. Canals drawn from the Chu River, including the ancient Krasnorechensky canal network, distributed water across broad alluvial terraces between the northern slopes of the Kyrgyz Ala-Too and the desert margins of the Moiynkum, creating a continuous 120-kilometre corridor of agricultural estates that sustained the fortified towns of Suyab, Navekat and Balasagun [@Elemanova2025Channels; @Franklin2023Archaeolog].

Sedentary demography relied upon complex hydraulic infrastructure maintained through institutional coordination [@MirMakhamad2023Testing; @Elemanova2025Channels]. Extensive canal systems (*anhār*) diverted river water across multiple terrace levels, regulated by wooden sluices, weirs and silt clearance regimes. In piedmont zones, subterranean filtration galleries (*qanats* or *karez*) tapped high water tables, conveying moisture to arid fan surfaces without evaporative loss [@MirMakhamad2023Testing; @Pardaev2019Design].

The agronomic foundation of the mediaeval population expansion was the diffusion of summer-cropped cultigens associated with the mediaeval Islamic green revolution [@MirMakhamad2023Testing; @MirMakhamad2024Agricultur]. Archaeobotanical assemblages across the Middle Zarafshan, Ferghana and the Chu Valley demonstrate that alongside traditional winter cereals (naked barley and free-threshing wheat), mediaeval cultivators adopted Asiatic cotton (*Gossypium herbaceum*), broomcorn and foxtail millets, hard rice (*Oryza sativa*), sorghum (*Sorghum bicolor*), sesame, watermelons, pomegranates and alfalfa [@MirMakhamad2023Testing; @MirMakhamad2024Agricultur; @Peters2024Archaeolog]. Cotton emerged as an industrial cash crop, fuelling textile manufacture across Mawarannahr and generating taxable agricultural surpluses that supported expanding city populations [@MirMakhamad2024Agricultur; @Uskinovna2024Spiritual].

## Sogdian City-States and Early Turkic Steppe Hegemonies (500AD to 700AD)

During Late Antiquity, prior to the Arab-Muslim conquest, Transoxiana was dominated by an Iranian agrarian and mercantile population organised into autonomous city-states collectively known as Sogdiana (*Sogd*) [@Garosi2025Frontier; @Zheng2025Gold]. The principal centres included Samarkand (Afrasiab), Bukhara, Panjakent, Kesh, Nasaf and Paykend [@MirMakhamad2024Agricultur; @Zheng2025Gold]. Each city-state was governed by an aristocratic ruler (*ikhshid* or *afshin*), supported by landed gentry (*dihqans*) and merchant guilds (*chakar*) [@Garosi2025Frontier; @Zheng2025Gold]. Sogdian merchants operated trans-continental commercial networks linking Sasanian Persia and Byzantium to Chang'an and Luoyang, controlling the luxury trade in silk, musk, precious gems and silver plate [@Zheng2025Gold; @Franklin2023Archaeolog].

The countryside surrounding these urban nodes was densely occupied by fortified aristocratic manor estates (*koshk*) and rural hamlets [@MirMakhamad2024Agricultur; @Garosi2025Frontier]. Archaeological surveys in the Zarafshan valley reveal hundreds of mudbrick castles featuring two-storey towers, crenellated parapets and central residential courtyards inhabited by *dihqan* lineages. In the upper mountain reaches of the Zarafshan, mountain redoubts such as Mount Mug served as administrative repositories and defensive refuges, as evidenced by the archive of Divashtich, which preserves legal contracts, tax rolls and correspondence in Sogdian script [@Garosi2025Frontier; @MirMakhamad2024Agricultur].

Prior to the consolidation of the Western Turkic Khaganate, the fifth-century hegemony of the Hephthalite confederation linked Transoxiana with Tokharistan (Bactria) and northern India, stimulating early urban monetization [@Wang2025Ancient; @GnecchiRuscone2025Ancient]. The Hephthalites minted debased silver drachms imitating Sasanian prototypes of King Peroz, which were subsequently countermarked by local Sogdian city rulers and Western Turkic governors. Epigraphic evidence from Bactrian legal documents and Sogdian inscriptions in the Talas and Chu valleys confirms that elite lineages utilized both Sogdian and Bactrian cursive scripts for international treaties, property deeds and slave conveyances, demonstrating an integrated trans-regional administrative culture across the Oxus-Jaxartes divide [@Garosi2025Frontier; @GnecchiRuscone2024Network].

In the mid-sixth century, the pastoralist Ashina clan established the First Turkic Khaganate, followed by the Western Turkic Khaganate, extending pastoralist hegemony across the northern steppe, Semirechye and the oasis kingdoms of Transoxiana [@Knar2024Turkic; @Knar2024Turkicb; @Wang2025Ancient]. This interaction produced a dynamic nomadic-sedentary symbiosis [@Knar2024Turkic; @Franklin2023Archaeolog]. The Western Turkic khagans established their seasonal capitals in the fertile valleys of Semirechye (Suyab and Navakat) and Chach, leaving local Sogdian civic administrations intact in exchange for tribute, trade concessions and diplomatic services [@Knar2024Turkicb; @Garosi2025Frontier].

Urban landscapes in this era were characterised by fortified citadels (*kuhandiz*) and walled residential cores (*shahristan*), decorated with polychrome palace frescoes, wood carvings and Zoroastrian ossuaries, alongside flourishing Nestorian Christian, Manichaean and Buddhist communities [@kyzy2025Religious; @Franklin2023Archaeolog; @Zheng2025Gold]. Total domain population in 500AD stood at 3,55M, with the Mawarannahr core holding 745,5k inhabitants, Ferghana supporting 568k, Chach holding 461,5k, and Merv sustaining 426k. By 650AD, sustained mercantile prosperity lifted aggregate headcount to 4,1M.

## The Arab Conquest of Mawarannahr and Early Islamisation (700AD to 820AD)

The westward expansion of the Umayyad Caliphate reached the Oxus frontier in the late seventh century [@Garosi2025Frontier]. Beginning in 705AD, the Umayyad general Qutayba ibn Muslim launched systemic military campaigns north of the river, subjugating Bukhara, Samarkand, Khwarazm, Chach and Ferghana [@Garosi2025Frontier; @Ilxomovna2026Reconstruc]. The conquest encountered protracted resistance: local Sogdian princes, led by Divashtich of Panjakent and Ghurak of Samarkand, repeatedly allied with the nomadic Turgesh Khaganate to expel Arab garrisons [@Garosi2025Frontier; @Knar2024Turkicb].

The conquest triggered deep restructuring of urban space and religious practice [@kyzy2025Religious; @Garosi2025Frontier]. In major urban cores, Arab garrisons were billeted inside residential quarters, while ancient Zoroastrian fire temples and administrative plazas were progressively transformed into Friday congregational mosques (*masjid-i jami*), as seen at Bukhara and Samarkand. Along the outer fringes of the cultivated oases, fortified border monasteries and garrison outposts (*ribat*) were erected to defend sedentary peasant communities against pagan nomadic raids from the northern steppes, establishing the architectural prototype for subsequent urban caravanserais [@Roberts2024Using; @Franklin2023Archaeolog].

The decisive geopolitical turning point occurred in July 751AD at the Battle of Talas (Atlakh), situated near modern Taraz [@Knar2024Turkicb; @Anon2024Buran]. An Abbasid army allied with Karluk Turkic forces decisively defeated a Tang expeditionary force commanded by Gao Xianzhi [@Knar2024Turkic; @Garosi2025Frontier]. This victory checked Chinese imperial ambitions in Central Asia, ensured Islamic political primacy across Mawarannahr, and facilitated the transmission of Chinese papermaking technology to Samarkand, which rapidly became the pre-eminent paper manufacturing centre of the Islamic world [@Garosi2025Frontier; @Ainakulov2024Influence].

The incorporation of Transoxiana into the Abbasid Caliphate altered regional administrative structures [@Garosi2025Frontier; @Ruhullah2025Leadership]. Arabic became the primary language of fiscal administration and religious scholarship, though Middle Persian and local Sogdian vernaculars persisted in daily commerce [@Garosi2025Frontier]. Gradual conversion to Islam accelerated as fiscal exemptions (*jizya* relief) were extended to Muslim converts and local *dihqans* integrated into imperial administrative hierarchies [@kyzy2025Religious; @Ruhullah2025Leadership]. Despite localized disruption during the conquest, regional demographic growth resumed: by 800AD, domain population reached 4,45M, supported by expanding trade along renewed trans-Eurasian caravan routes [@Franklin2023Archaeolog; @MOLDAGALIYEVA2024Socio].

The administrative transition from Sogdian chanceries to the Arabic fiscal apparatus was gradual and complex [@Garosi2025Frontier]. Across Mawarannahr, bilingual scribes initially drafted parallel receipts and tax registers in both Arabic and Sogdian, utilising the cursive Aramaic-derived Sogdian alphabet for local village rolls and grain weigh-bills while communicating with the central caliphal exchequer in Kufa and Baghdad in Arabic [@Garosi2025Frontier; @Gunduz2026Journey]. It was not until the administrative reforms of the late eighth century and the appointment of the Barmakid viziers that Arabic established definitive supremacy in official state correspondence, leaving Sogdian to retreat into montane valleys such as the Yagnob, where an archaic dialect survived into modern times [@Garosi2025Frontier; @Ainakulov2024Influence].

## The Samanid Flourishing and Agrarian Intensification (819AD to 999AD)

The ninth and tenth centuries witnessed the zenith of mediaeval Central Asian urbanism under the Samanid dynasty (819AD to 999AD), an indigenous Persianate Sunni regime descended from the Sogdian nobility of Balkh [@Ruhullah2025Leadership; @Uskinovna2024Spiritual]. Operating as semi-autonomous governors under Abbasid suzerainty, the Samanid amirs established their capital at Bukhara (*Bukhara-i Sharif*) and elevated Samarkand into a secondary imperial metropolis [@kyzy2025Religious; @Uskinovna2024Spiritual].

Under Samanid rule, Central Asia functioned as the intellectual and scientific engine of the Islamic world [@Ainakulov2024Influence; @Gunduz2026Journey]. The royal court and regional libraries supported polymaths including Al-Khwarizmi, Al-Farabi, Al-Biruni and Ibn Sina (Avicenna), alongside pioneering Persian literary figures such as Rudaki and Ferdowsi [@Ainakulov2024Influence]. Urban centres expanded rapidly beyond their ancient walls: the traditional bipartite division (*kuhandiz* and *shahristan*) gave way to sprawling artisan and commercial suburbs (*rabad*), which were enclosed in monumental defensive walls, such as Bukhara's monumental rampart (*Divar-i Kundak*) built to deter steppe raids [@Roberts2024Using; @Pardaev2019Design].

Specialised manufacturing flourished across the Samanid realm [@Franklin2023Archaeolog; @Uskinovna2024Spiritual]. Samarkand was renowned across Afro-Eurasia for high-grade rag paper and glazed polychrome slipware ceramics decorated with Arabic epigraphy, while Chach manufactured iron weaponry and leather goods, and Ferghana operated extensive silver and copper mines in the Kurama mountains [@Pardaev2019Design; @Franklin2023Archaeolog]. Municipal governance was administered through professional bureaus headed by the city prefect (*rais*) and market supervisor (*muhtasib*), who regulated fair trading practices, canal upkeep and public sanitation [@Roberts2024Using; @Ruhullah2025Leadership].

The Samanid state minted millions of high-purity silver dirhams (*Isma'ili dirhams*), which circulated as international commercial currency from northern Europe to China, as attested by massive hoard finds across Scandinavia and Rus lands [@Franklin2023Archaeolog; @Zheng2025Gold]. Concurrently, agricultural production intensified through royal investment in diversion dams, aqueducts and storage reservoirs [@MirMakhamad2023Testing; @Elemanova2025Channels]. By 950AD, domain population reached 5,55M, representing a 24,7% expansion over 800AD baselines. Mawarannahr Core held 1,17M inhabitants (density 5,34 persons per km²), Ferghana supported 888k, and the Khurasan frontier reached 666k.

## Karakhanid, Seljuk and Khwarazmshah Zenith (999AD to 1219AD)

In the late tenth century, the conversion of the Karluk and Yaghma Turkic confederations to Islam under Sultan Satuq Bughra Khan led to the formation of the Karakhanid Khaganate (*Qarakhanids*) [@Knar2024Turkic; @kyzy2025Religious; @Anon2024Buran]. In 999AD, the Karakhanids captured Bukhara, dividing the former Samanid realm along the Amu Darya in partition with the Ghaznavids [@Knar2024Turkic; @Anon2024Buran]. The Karakhanids established dual capitals at Balasagun in the Chu Valley and Kashgar, with a Western Karakhanid branch ruling Samarkand, Bukhara, Uzgen and Akhsikent [@Anon2024Buran; @Elemanova2025Channels].

The political consolidation of the Karakhanid Khaganate institutionalised seasonal transhumance routes that integrated northern steppe pastoralism with southern urban markets [@Knar2024Turkic; @MOLDAGALIYEVA2024Socio]. Pastoralist clans spent winter months in sheltered lowlands along the Syr Darya and Chu rivers (*qystau*), trading wool, hides, meat and horses for agricultural grain and woven textiles in border market towns such as Otrar, Sayram and Taraz, before migrating to lush subalpine pastures (*zhailau*) in the Tian Shan during summer [@Knar2024Turkic; @Elemanova2025Channels]. This economic integration fostered bilingual Turkic-Persian urban cultures and expanded civic revenue [@Gunduz2026Journey; @Anon2024Buran].

Karakhanid rule accelerated the linguistic Turkification of Central Asian urban populations while preserving Islamic religious and Persian administrative structures [@Knar2024Turkic; @Gunduz2026Journey]. Monuments such as the Burana Minaret near Balasagun, the Uzgen mausolea and the Kalyan Minaret in Bukhara attest to monumental fired-brick architecture and sophisticated civic engineering [@Anon2024Buran; @kyzy2025Religious]. Sedentarisation of nomadic pastoralists in the Chu, Talas and Syr Darya valleys stimulated urban growth at Otrar, Sayram (Isfijab), Taraz and Sighnaq [@Knar2024Turkic; @MOLDAGALIYEVA2024Socio].

Simultaneously, the Oghuz Turkic migration southward established the Great Seljuk Empire in Khurasan [@Knar2024Turkic; @Roberts2024Using]. Under Alp Arslan and Sultan Sanjar, Merv (*Marw al-Shahijan*) became an imperial capital, expanding into a metropolis of 150.000 residents supported by an elaborate canal network fed by the Sultan Band dam across the Murghab River [@Roberts2024Using]. Following the decline of the Seljuks and Qara Khitai incursions in the twelfth century, the Khwarazmshah dynasty centered at Gurganj (Kunya-Urgench) and Kath unified Transoxiana, Khurasan and Khwarazm into an expansive empire [@Ilxomovna2026Reconstruc; @Sharipbayeva2026Geopolitic].

On the eve of the catastrophic Mongol campaigns led by Genghis Khan in 1219AD, mediaeval Central Asian urbanism reached its historic apex [@Sharipbayeva2026Geopolitic]. Total domain population peaked at 6,95M (6.950.000) across 3.890.946 km², with urban densities in Mawarannahr and Ferghana surpassing all preceding historical thresholds.

# Methodology

## Territorial Partition and Regional Framework

To capture the geographic, hydrological and political mosaic of mediaeval Central Asia without distortion, this study partitions the domain into nine territorial provinces encompassing 3.890.946 km² across 65.332 five-arcminute grid cells (Table \ref{tab:validation-turan}):

1. Mawarannahr Core: Bukhara, Samarkand, Kesh and Nasaf (218.084 km², 3.342 grid cells), covering the central Zarafshan and Kashkadarya basins.
2. Chach, Ilak, Isfijab and Otrar Frontier (332.610 km², 5.387 grid cells), spanning the middle Syr Darya, Angren and Chirchiq river systems.
3. Ferghana and Ustrushana: Akhsikent, Khujand and Uzgen (124.532 km², 1.907 grid cells), encompassing the fertile intermontane upper Syr Darya bowl.
4. Chaghaniyan, Khuttal and Badakhshan (129.573 km², 2.016 grid cells), covering the upper Amu Darya tributaries (Surxondaryo, Vakhsh, Panj) and high Pamir piedmonts.
5. Khwarazm: Gurganj and Kath (218.071 km², 3.432 grid cells), covering the lower Amu Darya delta and southern Aral basin.
6. Khurasan Frontier: Merv, Nisa, Amul and Dihistan (399.026 km², 5.930 grid cells), spanning the Murghab delta, Kopet Dag piedmont and southeastern Caspian shores.
7. Semirechye and Chu-Talas Karluk-Karakhanid Towns: Balasagun and Taraz (461.565 km², 7.556 grid cells), covering northern Tian Shan river basins draining into Lake Balkhash.
8. Oghuz and Western Kipchak Steppe: Aral, Ural and Mangyshlak (734.341 km², 12.648 grid cells), encompassing arid western pastoral rangelands.
9. Kimak-Kipchak Central and Northern Steppe (1.273.144 km², 23.114 grid cells), encompassing vast northern Eurasian grasslands drained by the Ishim, Irtysh and Tobol rivers.

At each historical benchmark year $t \in \{500, 650, 800, 950, 1100, 1200, 1219\}$, regional population $P_r(t)$ synthesises archaeological site registers, urban intramural hectarages, irrigation discharge balances, and pastoral nomadic carrying capacity envelopes:

$$P_r(t) = S_r(t) \cdot h_r(t) \cdot \omega_r(t) + F_r(t)$$

where $S_r(t)$ represents the number of active domestic urban and rural settlement nuclei, $h_r(t)$ is the mean household multiplier (calibrated between 5 and 6,2 persons per family unit), $\omega_r(t)$ is the residential contemporaneity and occupation coefficient, and $F_r(t)$ accounts for mobile pastoralist nomadic encampments operating outside permanent masonry architecture [@MirMakhamad2024Agricultur; @Roberts2024Using; @Knar2024Turkic].

## Multi-Proxy Demographic Calibration

Demographic estimation across mediaeval Central Asia requires integrating three primary data streams: urban structural surveys, mediaeval tax registers and geographical chronicles, and geostatistical irrigation capacity models [@Roberts2024Using; @Franklin2023Archaeolog; @MirMakhamad2023Testing].

Archaeological excavations conducted across Merv, Samarkand (Afrasiab), Bukhara, Kunya-Urgench, Otrar and Taraz provide empirical measurements of enclosed settlement surface areas [@Roberts2024Using; @Pardaev2019Design; @MOLDAGALIYEVA2024Socio]. Population densities within mediaeval walled cores (*shahristan*) are calibrated between 150 and 250 persons per hectare, accounting for multi-room mudbrick courtyard dwellings, narrow street grids, mosques and public baths [@Roberts2024Using]. Outer suburban zones (*rabad*), which contained extensive market gardens, caravanserai complexes and pottery kilns, supported lower densities of 35 to 80 persons per hectare [@Roberts2024Using; @Franklin2023Archaeolog].

Household size parameters ($h_r(t) = 5{,}0$ to $6{,}2$) are derived from architectural ground plans of excavated domestic compounds at Afrasiab, Panjakent, Otrar and Taraz [@Roberts2024Using; @Pardaev2019Design]. Mediaeval Central Asian residences typically comprised multi-generational extended families sharing a walled domestic compound with a central open courtyard, peripheral living quarters, domestic baking ovens (*tandir*), and storage vaults [@MirMakhamad2024Agricultur]. In rural villages, compound densities varied from 12 to 24 units per hectare, yielding village populations of 150 to 600 persons [@Roberts2024Using]. Contemporaneity correction factors ($\omega_r(t)$) account for the cyclic rebuilding of mudbrick walls, whose structural lifespan rarely exceeded two to three generations (40 to 60 years) without substantial wall reconstruction [@Roberts2024Using; @Ilxomovna2026Reconstruc].

For non-sedentary pastoralist populations ($F_r(t)$), demographic scaling accounts for seasonal transhumance patterns across the northern steppes and piedmont uplands [@Knar2024Turkic; @Wang2025Ancient]. Historical records of Turkic tribal levies (e.g. Karluks, Oghuz, Kimaks, Kipchaks) record military mobilization rates of approximately one mounted warrior per five to six family members [@Knar2024Turkicb; @Yaldz2023Political]. Combining camp counts recorded in early Islamic itineraries with livestock carrying capacity envelopes yields regional nomadic population densities ranging from 0,22 persons per km² across arid saxaul rangelands to 0,65 persons per km² in fertile subalpine valleys of the Chu and Talas rivers [@Knar2024Turkic; @Elemanova2025Channels].

These archaeological measurements are cross-referenced against mediaeval Arabic and Persian geographical compendia, notably the itineraries of Ibn Khordadbeh, Al-Istakhri, Ibn Hawqal, Al-Muqaddasi and Al-Biruni [@Garosi2025Frontier; @kyzy2025Religious]. These sources detail taxation receipts (*kharaj* and *jizya*), garrison complements, Friday mosque capacities, and the physical extent of irrigation networks [@kyzy2025Religious; @Ruhullah2025Leadership].

Hydrological models calibrate maximum demographic carrying capacities based on mean annual river discharge: the Zarafshan (average discharge 160 m³/s) supported a sustainable agricultural population ceiling of approximately 1,2M to 1,5M; the Murghab delta supported up to 800k; and the lower Amu Darya delta in Khwarazm sustained 700k to 900k [@MirMakhamad2023Testing; @Elemanova2025Channels; @Ilxomovna2026Reconstruc]. In northern pastoralist zones, nomadic densities are constrained to 0,2 to 0,5 persons per km² based on seasonal grazing turnover and livestock biomass carrying capacities [@Knar2024Turkic; @Wang2025Ancient].

## Non-Stationary Kriging and Biophysical Covariates

Spatial population allocation across the 65.332 grid cells is modelled using Paciorek-Schervish non-stationary Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) kriging [@Roberts2024Using], drawing upon 12.473 domestic assigned archaeological records across 442 domestic catchments. The non-stationary covariance between locations $s_i$ and $s_j$ is specified as:

$$C(s_i, s_j) = \sigma_i \sigma_j \, |\Sigma_i|^{1/4} |\Sigma_j|^{1/4} \left|\frac{\Sigma_i + \Sigma_j}{2}\right|^{-1/2} \mathcal{M}_{3/2}\!\left(\sqrt{Q_{ij}}\right)$$

The mathematical structure of the Paciorek-Schervish formulation allows local geometric anisotropy and spatial correlation lengths to vary continuously across complex topography [@Roberts2024Using]. The spatial kernel matrix $\Sigma_i$ at grid location $s_i$ is parameterised by local terrain ruggedness and river valley orientation, ensuring that spatial correlation decays rapidly across arid mountain ridges and desert escarpments whilst extending along linear fluvial channels [@Roberts2024Using; @Elemanova2025Channels]. The Matérn smoothness parameter $\nu = 3/2$ represents the optimal compromise between the non-differentiable roughness of an exponential model ($\nu = 1/2$) and the infinitely differentiable smoothness of a Gaussian model ($\nu \to \infty$), generating realistic once-differentiable population density surfaces that capture sharp oasis boundaries without introducing unphysical negative density oscillations [@Roberts2024Using].

Regularised variogram bandwidth parameters are established at $\tau_1 = 1{,}50$ and $\tau_2 = 2{,}775$, yielding effective short ranges of 71,04 km across all horizons (Table \ref{tab:kriging-turan}). The residual kriging model incorporates five environmental and accessibility covariates: habitable land fraction ($\beta_{\text{hab}}$), natural vegetative productivity index ($\beta_{\text{nat}}$), terrain ecozone suitability ($\beta_{\text{eco}}$), fluvial proximity decay ($\beta_{\text{fluvial}}$), and coastal or lacustrine proximity ($\beta_{\text{coastal}}$). Dense urban settlement cores from 1.029 catalogued sites are protected by urban mask buffers to prevent distortion of underlying rural density surfaces [@Roberts2024Using; @Pardaev2019Design].

The 14 source registries aggregated in Table \ref{tab:source-corpora-turan} represent the comprehensive state of archaeological and toponymic documentation across Central Asia [@Franklin2023Archaeolog; @MOLDAGALIYEVA2024Socio]. UCL CAAL registers contribute 22.454 monuments and dated horizons across Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Kyrgyzstan, alongside the national heritage registries of the Uzbekistan Cabinet of Ministers (Resolution No. 846, 6.156 monuments) and Kazakhstan Ministry of Culture (Order No. 88, 185 sites), and the Harvard Published Excavations Atlas (2.642 records), providing the spatial baseline for domestic catchment interpolation. These records are harmonised with 827 classical Islamic toponyms from the Al-Thurayya gazetteer, 1.613 classical sites from Pleiades, 2.317 canal and settlement nodes from ArchAtlas, and 1.346 radiocarbon determinations from the c14bazAAR/p3k14c database [@Franklin2023Archaeolog; @kyzy2025Religious]. Spatial deduplication and coordinate verification ensure that each catalogued settlement corresponds to a discrete archaeological core with verified occupation spans.

# Results

## Late Antique and Early Turkic Oases (500AD to 800AD)

Between 500AD and 800AD, the population of Turan and Transoxiana experienced steady expansion, rising from 3,55M to 4,45M despite the political turmoil of the Arab conquest (Figure \ref{fig:traj-turan}). In 500AD, the Core Transoxiana oases (Mawarannahr Core, Chach and Ferghana) supported 1,78M people, representing exactly 50% of the total domain population.

<figure class="crd-figure-block" id="fig:traj-turan">
<img class="crd-figure-img" src="/artefacts/project_saray/1.0-turkic-migrations-and-islamisation-turan/fig2_turkic_migrations_and_islamisation_turan_trajectory.png" alt="fig:traj-turan" loading="lazy" />
<figcaption class="crd-caption"><span class="crd-caption-label">Figure 2.</span> Demographic trajectory of mediaeval Turan and Transoxiana from 500AD to 1219AD across nine provinces with historical uncertainty intervals.</figcaption>
</figure>

The Mawarannahr core flourished as the commercial fulcrum of Eurasian overland trade [@Zheng2025Gold; @Franklin2023Archaeolog]. Samarkand maintained a population of 45.000 in 500AD, expanding to 65.000 by 650AD, while Bukhara grew from 35.000 to 48.000 [@Roberts2024Using]. Along the southern river corridors, Merv anchored an urban oasis of 60.000 in 500AD, rising to 75.000 by 650AD [@Roberts2024Using].

During the eighth century, military clashes between Umayyad armies, local Sogdian confederacies and Turgesh nomads temporarily depressed rural production in the Zarafshan and Kashkadarya valleys [@Garosi2025Frontier; @Knar2024Turkicb]. However, the consolidation of Abbasid rule following the Battle of Talas in 751AD and the pacification of regional trade routes triggered rapid demographic recovery [@Knar2024Turkic; @Anon2024Buran]. By 800AD, total domain population attained 4,45M, with Mawarannahr Core reaching 934,5k, Ferghana supporting 712k, Chach holding 578,5k, and Khurasan sustaining 534k.

The divergent ecological foundations of the nine provinces shaped regional growth rates during the early mediaeval centuries [@Roberts2024Using; @Knar2024Turkic]. While the core irrigation zones of Mawarannahr, Ferghana and Merv expanded under intensive canal cultivation, the peripheral steppe provinces (Oghuz-Kipchak and Kimak-Kipchak) maintained extensive pastoralist adaptations characterised by low aggregate densities (0,19 to 0,21 persons per km²). In these northern grasslands, pastoral mobility was essential to cope with extreme seasonal temperature fluctuations and periodic winter blizzards (*dzhut*), which decimated livestock herds and induced episodic migration southward toward the Syr Darya frontier [@Knar2024Turkic; @Wang2025Ancient]. In contrast, the montane valleys of Chaghaniyan, Khuttal and Badakhshan along the upper Amu Darya supported stable terraced agriculture, fruit orchards and lapis lazuli and ruby mining, lifting population from 319,5k in 500AD to 400,5k in 800AD [@Franklin2023Archaeolog; @Zheng2025Gold].

## The Samanid Urban Renaissance and Agrarian Expansion (800AD to 1000AD)

The period between 800AD and 1000AD witnessed the fastest sustained demographic growth in mediaeval Central Asian history (Figure \ref{fig:density-turan}). Total domain population surged by 24,7%, climbing from 4,45M in 800AD to 5,55M in 950AD.

<figure class="crd-figure-block" id="fig:density-turan">
<img class="crd-figure-img" src="/artefacts/project_saray/1.0-turkic-migrations-and-islamisation-turan/fig3_turkic_migrations_and_islamisation_turan_density.png" alt="fig:density-turan" loading="lazy" />
<figcaption class="crd-caption"><span class="crd-caption-label">Figure 3.</span> Continuous kriged population density surface and territorial density comparison across mediaeval Turan and Transoxiana.</figcaption>
</figure>

This expansion was propelled by intensive agricultural engineering and the rapid commercialisation of oasis economies under Samanid administration [@MirMakhamad2023Testing; @MirMakhamad2024Agricultur]. Cotton production expanded dramatically along the Zarafshan and Syr Darya, stimulating extensive urban manufacturing in Bukhara, Samarkand and Chach (Tashkent) [@MirMakhamad2024Agricultur; @Uskinovna2024Spiritual]. By 950AD, Samarkand and Bukhara each sustained 95.000 residents, placing them among the largest urban metropolises of the Islamic world alongside Baghdad, Cairo and Cordoba [@Roberts2024Using; @kyzy2025Religious].

In Khwarazm, hydraulic expansion along the lower Amu Darya supported 610,5k inhabitants across Gurganj and Kath [@Ilxomovna2026Reconstruc; @Ilniyazovich2023Karakalpak]. Along the Syr Darya frontier, Chach, Ilak and Isfijab reached 721,5k residents, functioning as the primary commercial interface between Islamic urban merchants and pastoral nomads from the Kimak-Kipchak steppe [@MOLDAGALIYEVA2024Socio; @Knar2024Turkic].

The spatial density surface generated through non-stationary kriging illustrates the extreme concentration of mediaeval population within irrigated oasis perimeters [@Roberts2024Using]. In the Zarafshan delta, rural population densities reached 28 to 45 persons per km², comparable to contemporaneous agricultural lowlands in the Nile Valley and Mesopotamia, whilst surrounding Kyzylkum desert tracts sustained densities well below 0,1 persons per km² [@MirMakhamad2024Agricultur; @Roberts2024Using].

The archaeological footprint of Samanid urban expansion is confirmed by the proliferation of secondary craft and market towns across Ustrushana and Ferghana [@Pardaev2019Design; @kyzy2025Religious]. Sites such as Jizax (Dzhizak), Zomin, Akhsikent and Uzgen expanded from minor fortified villages into substantial commercial centres featuring fired-brick bathhouses (*hammam*), metal smelting workshops, and multi-domed mosques [@Pardaev2019Design; @kyzy2025Religious]. At Akhsikent on the northern bank of the Syr Darya, excavations reveal specialised steel crucible furnaces producing Damascus steel blades exported across the Islamic world, demonstrating the high degree of technical and industrial specialisation sustaining urban agglomerations [@Pardaev2019Design; @Franklin2023Archaeolog].

## Karakhanid, Seljuk and Khwarazmshah Zenith (1000AD to 1219AD)

Over the final two centuries prior to the Mongol conquest, Central Asian population expanded from 5,55M in 950AD to 6,35M in 1100AD, reaching 6,85M in 1200AD and attaining an apex of 6,95M in 1219AD (Table \ref{tab:regions-turan}).

In Khurasan, Merv experienced monumental expansion under Seljuk imperial patronage, reaching 145.000 inhabitants in 1100AD and 150.000 in 1200AD, supported by Sultan Sanjar's irrigation investments and expansive suburban caravanserais [@Roberts2024Using]. In Mawarannahr, Samarkand grew to 110.000 in 1100AD and 120.000 on the eve of the Mongol siege in 1219AD, while Bukhara sustained 100.000 residents [@Roberts2024Using]. In Khwarazm, the imperial capital of Kunya-Urgench expanded to 75.000 in 1100AD and 95.000 in 1200AD, reflecting the immense wealth and geopolitical dominance of the Khwarazmshah Empire [@Ilxomovna2026Reconstruc; @Sharipbayeva2026Geopolitic].

In Semirechye and the Chu-Talas basin, Karakhanid pastoralist-urban synthesis sustained 556k inhabitants by 1219AD, anchored by urban centres at Balasagun (32.000) and Taraz (32.000) [@Anon2024Buran; @Elemanova2025Channels]. Across the northern steppes, the Kimak and Kipchak confederations supported 417k mobile pastoralists, while the Oghuz-Kipchak western steppe held 278k inhabitants [@Knar2024Turkic; @Wang2025Ancient].

The pre-Mongol zenith of 1219AD represented the historic carrying-capacity ceiling of Central Asian pre-industrial hydraulic engineering [@MirMakhamad2023Testing; @Roberts2024Using]. The aggregate headcount of 6,95M was supported by near-continuous canal corridors along the Zarafshan and Kashkadarya, dense networks of walled garden estates in Ferghana, and thousands of flourishing caravanserais linking Transoxiana to the wider Islamic and Eurasian world [@Franklin2023Archaeolog; @MOLDAGALIYEVA2024Socio; @Sharipbayeva2026Geopolitic].

Following their defeat of the Seljuk sultan Sanjar at the Battle of Qatwan in 1141AD, the non-Muslim Khitan dynasty of the Qara Khitai established imperial suzerainty over Transoxiana and Semirechye [@Knar2024Turkic; @Anon2024Buran]. Unlike previous conquest regimes, the Qara Khitai Gurkhans maintained a policy of indirect rule, avoiding direct military occupation of Muslim cities and refraining from confiscating agricultural lands. They stationed imperial tax collectors (*shangjian*) outside urban walls and collected fixed annual tributes while permitting Muslim governors and religious authorities to administer local affairs autonomously [@Knar2024Turkic; @Gunduz2026Journey]. This institutional arrangement ensured uninterrupted agricultural production and continued demographic growth through the mid-twelfth century, providing the demographic and economic base subsequently inherited by the Khwarazmshah Empire [@Ilxomovna2026Reconstruc; @Sharipbayeva2026Geopolitic].

## Urban Hierarchy and Settlement Dynamics

The mediaeval settlement network of Turan and Transoxiana exhibited a highly integrated rank-size distribution. Out of 1.029 catalogued settlement nodes, the primary urban tier comprised four metropolises exceeding 90.000 inhabitants: Merv (150.000), Samarkand (120.000), Bukhara (100.000) and Kunya-Urgench (95.000) [@Roberts2024Using; @Ilxomovna2026Reconstruc].

A dense second tier of provincial capitals supported populations between 25.000 and 50.000, including Old Termez (50.000), Tashkent (48.000), Otrar (40.000), Khujand (38.000), Taraz (35.000), Akhsikent (35.000), Balasagun (32.000), Sayram (30.000), Amul (26.000), Uzgen (26.000) and Shahrisabz (25.000) [@Roberts2024Using; @Anon2024Buran; @MOLDAGALIYEVA2024Socio; @Pardaev2019Design].

Below these major centres lay hundreds of fortified market towns, caravanserai stations and agricultural villages spaced at daily marching intervals (25 to 35 kilometres) along trans-Eurasian trade routes [@Franklin2023Archaeolog; @MOLDAGALIYEVA2024Socio]. The spacing of intermediate stations reflects the operational logistics of camel caravans travelling across desert and steppe environments. Along the northern Silk Road connecting Samarkand to Chach (Tashkent), Isfijab (Sayram), Taraz and Balasagun, fortified roadside caravanserais provided animal fodder, secure storage vaults, brick water reservoirs (*sardoba*) and customs inspection posts [@Franklin2023Archaeolog; @Anon2024Buran]. Prominent monuments such as Rabati Malik between Samarkand and Bukhara, Dayahatyn along the middle Amu Darya, and the stone caravanserai of Tash Rabat in the Tian Shan passes illustrate the massive architectural investments dedicated to securing trade corridors [@Franklin2023Archaeolog; @Uskinovna2024Spiritual].

Each caravanserai sustained a resident garrison, craft repair workshops and service personnel of 100 to 400 individuals, functioning as permanent miniature service towns embedded in arid landscapes [@Franklin2023Archaeolog; @MOLDAGALIYEVA2024Socio]. In the Kopet Dag piedmont corridor of Khurasan, a chain of fortified towns including Nisa, Abivard and Dandanakan protected the southern caravan route linking Nishapur to Merv, facilitating the transit of silk, turquoise and luxury metalwork [@Roberts2024Using; @Zheng2025Gold].

This hierarchical network facilitated the collection of agricultural surplus, the redistribution of industrial manufactured goods, and rapid communications across the oasis landscape, creating an urban system of unprecedented resilience that endured until its abrupt destruction in 1219AD [@Sharipbayeva2026Geopolitic]. The aggregate archaeological evidence from 1.029 catalogued nodes demonstrates that urbanism in pre-Mongol Turan and Transoxiana was not merely a cluster of isolated riverine enclaves, but a deeply articulated, multi-tiered urban continuum spanning from the Caspian Sea to the Tian Shan [@Roberts2024Using; @Franklin2023Archaeolog].
